title: 22. Interview: Senior RAG & System Design Interview Bank (Part 1) (Part 1)
summary: Interview Q&A for Senior RAG & System Design Interview Bank (Part 1) — 27 questions with model answers (part 1 of 2).
objectives: Answer 27 Senior RAG & System Design Interview Bank (Part 1) interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
**Target Roles:** AI Engineer | AIML Engineer | Agentic AI Engineer | Generative AI Engineer
**File:** 1 of 4 | **Questions:** 50 (System Design)
**Skills Covered:** RAG, Vector Databases, Azure AI Search, FAISS, ChromaDB, LangChain, LangGraph, FastAPI, Scaling, Distributed Systems

sections.title: Q1. Million-User RAG Chatbot with Document Uploads
sections.body:
**Question:** You are building a RAG chatbot where users can upload documents. If a million users come to your endpoint simultaneously and upload documents, how would you design the system to handle this load?

**Explanation:** A synchronous upload-and-index pipeline would immediately collapse under a million concurrent requests because embedding generation and vector DB ingestion are CPU/GPU-bound and slow (seconds per document). The senior-level answer is to decouple upload from processing using an asynchronous event-driven architecture. The upload endpoint should only validate the file, store it in blob storage, and enqueue a job message. Background workers then pull jobs, chunk, embed, and upsert into the vector DB at their own pace. This pattern is the backbone of every production GenAI platform (OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, AWS Bedrock all use it).

**Visual Explanation:**
```
[1M Users] → [CDN/WAF] → [Load Balancer] → [FastAPI App (Auto-scaled 100+ pods)]
                                            ↓
                                   [Azure Blob Storage] (raw docs)
                                            ↓
                                   [Azure Service Bus / Kafka] (job queue)
                                            ↓
[Vector DB (AI Search)] ← [Embedding Workers (GPU pool)] ← [Chunking Workers]
       ↓
[RAG Query Service] ← [User Query]
```

**Step-by-Step Explanation:**
1. **Edge layer:** Put Azure Front Door / Cloudflare in front for TLS, WAF, rate limiting per IP/user (e.g., 5 uploads/min).
2. **API layer:** Deploy FastAPI behind Azure App Service autoscale (or AKS HPA). Stateless — no session affinity. Target P95 < 500ms for the upload acknowledgement.
3. **Storage:** Stream upload directly to Azure Blob Storage using SAS URLs or pre-signed URLs so the API server never buffers the full file in memory.
4. **Queue:** Publish a message to Azure Service Bus / Kafka with `{user_id, doc_id, blob_url, metadata}`. Use partitioned topics keyed by `user_id` for ordered per-user processing.
5. **Worker pools:** Separate "chunking workers" (CPU) from "embedding workers" (GPU). Scale independently based on queue depth (KEDA on Kubernetes).
6. **Embedding:** Batch documents (e.g., 32 chunks per call) to Azure OpenAI `text-embedding-3-large`. Cache embeddings in Redis to avoid re-embedding duplicates (content hash).
7. **Vector DB:** Use Azure AI Search with a semantic index. Upsert with retry + exponential backoff. Shard by tenant/user for very large indexes.
8. **Status callback:** Store job state in CosmosDB / Postgres. Frontend polls or receives a SignalR/WebSocket push when indexing completes.
9. **Failure handling:** Dead-letter queue after 3 retries. Alert on DLQ depth. Idempotent workers (check `doc_id` status before processing).
10. **Cost control:** Quota per user tier (free/paid). Spot instances for non-urgent batches. Store raw docs in Cool/Archive tier after 30 days.

sections.title: Q2. Million-Document Bulk Ingestion — Fast Approach
sections.body:
**Question:** Your organization has a million legacy documents that need to be ingested into a vector database. Leadership wants it done "quickly." How do you design a fast ingestion pipeline?

**Explanation:** Naive sequential ingestion of 1M docs at ~2s/doc = 23 days. The senior answer is a horizontally parallel, GPU-saturated, batched pipeline. The key levers are: (a) embarrassingly parallel chunking on CPU workers, (b) batched embedding calls to maximize GPU utilization, (c) parallel vector DB upserts with bulk APIs, (d) deduplication by content hash to skip re-embedding, and (e) skipping re-embedding unchanged docs on re-runs. Use Spark or Dask for the chunking fan-out if the org already has it; otherwise Kubernetes Jobs with a queue.

**Visual Explanation:**
```
[1M Docs in Blob/Data Lake]
        ↓
[Spark / Dask Fan-out — 200 workers] → chunking + hashing
        ↓
[Dedup via Redis content-hash cache] — skip already-embedded
        ↓
[Embedding Batch Pool — 8× GPU, batch=64] → Azure OpenAI / open-source
        ↓
[Bulk Upsert — 50 parallel writers] → Azure AI Search / Pinecone
        ↓
[Progress Tracker (CosmosDB)] + [DLQ for failures]
```

**Step-by-Step Explanation:**
1. **Inventory:** List all 1M docs, compute SHA-256 of each. Store manifest in Data Lake as Parquet.
2. **Dedup:** Outer-join manifest against an "already_ingested" table. Skip the ~30% that are duplicates or unchanged.
3. **Chunking fan-out:** Use PySpark on a 50-node cluster (Databricks / Synapse / self-managed K8s). Each task handles ~20k docs, produces chunks with deterministic IDs.
4. **Embedding:** Call Azure OpenAI in batches of 64 with concurrency=20 per GPU worker. 8× A100 workers → ~160 concurrent batches. Throughput ≈ 10k chunks/sec.
5. **Vector DB:** Use Azure AI Search `IndexDocumentsBatch` (up to 1000 docs/batch). 50 parallel writer pods. Disable indexing sync mode during bulk load, rebuild index at end.
6. **Checkpointing:** Commit progress every 10k docs. Restartable — if a worker dies, the next picks up from the last checkpoint.
7. **Validation:** Sample 1% of chunks post-ingest, query them back, verify recall > 95%.
8. **Time estimate:** With this design 1M docs finish in ~4–8 hours vs 23 days naive.
9. **Cost:** Spot/low-priority VMs for chunking, reserved GPU for embedding. Estimated $500–$1500.
10. **Cutover:** Blue-green index swap — build new index, alias switch, delete old.

sections.title: Q3. Multi-Tenant Vector DB Isolation
sections.body:
**Question:** Design a RAG system serving 1000 enterprise tenants. How do you isolate vector data per tenant in the vector database?

**Explanation:** Three canonical patterns exist: (1) **Shared index + filter** — cheapest, all tenants in one index, filter by `tenant_id` metadata. Risk: noisy neighbor, accidental leakage if filter is forgotten. (2) **Shared index + partition key** — AI Search supports a "semantic" partition key that physically co-locates a tenant's vectors. Better. (3) **Index-per-tenant** — strongest isolation, highest cost, ops overhead. Senior answer: tier tenants — small tenants on shared+filter, large/regulated tenants on dedicated indexes. Always enforce `tenant_id` filter at the query layer via middleware, never trust the caller.

**Visual Explanation:**
```
Tier 1 (Small tenants, <10k docs)    →  [Shared Index] + mandatory tenant_id filter
Tier 2 (Mid tenants, 10k–1M docs)    →  [Shared Index] + partition_key=tenant_id
Tier 3 (Enterprise/regulated)        →  [Dedicated Index per tenant] + VNet + CMK
                                          ↓
                            [Query Router] reads tenant config → routes to correct index
```

**Step-by-Step Explanation:**
1. **Tenant classification:** Store tenant tier in config DB (CosmosDB). Re-classify monthly based on doc count.
2. **Onboarding:** New tenant → shared index by default. Provision dedicated index only when tier-3 criteria met.
3. **Ingestion:** Embedding worker reads `tenant_id` from job, writes to the correct index/partition. Fail loudly if `tenant_id` missing.
4. **Query layer:** A `TenantAwareRetriever` LangChain wrapper ALWAYS injects `tenant_id` filter. Unit test that queries without tenant_id throw.
5. **Authorization:** JWT claim contains `tenant_id`. Validate at API gateway + retriever. Defense in depth.
6. **Key management:** Tier-3 tenants get Customer-Managed Keys (CMK) in Azure Key Vault. Rotate annually.
7. **Audit logging:** Log every query with tenant_id, user, doc_ids returned. Send to Log Analytics / Sentinel.
8. **Performance:** Monitor per-tenant query latency. Move noisy tenants to dedicated index if they degrade shared index.
9. **Data residency:** EU tenants → EU region index. US tenants → US region. Cross-region replication only with consent.
10. **Offboarding:** Tenant churn → delete their partition/index, verify zero residual vectors via audit query.

sections.title: Q4. Real-Time RAG with Sub-Second Latency
sections.body:
**Question:** Design a RAG chatbot that must answer user queries in under 800ms P95, including LLM generation.

**Explanation:** Standard RAG (embed query → vector search → LLM) easily exceeds 3s. To hit 800ms P95, every stage must be optimized. Key techniques: (a) semantic cache for repeat queries (Redis), (b) streaming LLM output so first-token latency matters not full latency, (c) smaller reranker or skip reranking, (d) GPU-accelerated embedding model colocated with API, (e) precomputed prompt prefix caching, (f) lower `max_tokens`, (g) prompt compression. The acceptance criterion becomes **time-to-first-token (TTFT)** < 300ms, not full response time.

**Visual Explanation:**
```
User Query
   ↓ (<5ms)
[Semantic Cache (Redis)] —hit→ return cached answer (<50ms)
   ↓ miss
[Embedding (local GPU, 10ms)] → [Vector Search (AI Search, 80ms)]
   ↓
[Optional Reranker (Cohere, 100ms) — skip if TTFT budget tight]
   ↓
[LLM Stream (Azure OpenAI, TTFT 250ms, 30 tok/s)] → stream to user
```
Budget: 10 + 80 + 100 + 250 = 440ms TTFT ✓

**Step-by-Step Explanation:**
1. **Embedding:** Self-host `bge-small-en` on GPU colocated with FastAPI. 10ms vs 80ms remote.
2. **Vector DB:** Azure AI Search with `Standard S1` tier, semantic ranker disabled for hot path (use pure vector). Cache top-100 results per query.
3. **Semantic cache:** Hash normalized query → Redis. Also store embedding + similarity threshold 0.95 for near-duplicate hits.
4. **LLM streaming:** Use Azure OpenAI `stream=True`. Stream tokens via SSE to frontend. TTFT is what the user perceives.
5. **Prompt caching:** Azure OpenAI caches prompt prefix automatically if >1024 tokens. Put system prompt + retrieved context first.
6. **Token budget:** `max_tokens=256`, `temperature=0.3`. Stop sequence on `\n\nUser:`.
7. **Reranker:** Make it optional. If TTFT budget allows, add Cohere rerank on top-20 → top-5. Otherwise skip.
8. **Connection pooling:** Reuse HTTP connections to Azure OpenAI. `httpx.AsyncClient` with `limits=max_keepalive=100`.
9. **Autoscaling:** HPA on `ttft_p95` custom metric. Scale FastAPI pods when P95 > 400ms.
10. **Fallback:** If LLM times out at 2s, return retrieved docs as "sources" with a templated answer. Graceful degradation.

sections.title: Q5. Hybrid Search Architecture
sections.body:
**Question:** A customer reports that pure vector search misses obvious keyword matches (e.g., product codes "SKU-12345"). How do you redesign the retrieval to handle this?

**Explanation:** Pure dense embeddings are weak at exact lexical matches (SKUs, IDs, names, error codes). The senior solution is **hybrid search**: combine BM25 sparse retrieval with dense vector retrieval, then fuse with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) or a learned reranker. Azure AI Search has native hybrid + RRF support. For self-hosted, run BM25 (Elasticsearch / OpenSearch) alongside FAISS, fuse scores, then rerank with a cross-encoder. Also: store exact-match fields as filterable metadata so users can hard-filter by SKU.

**Visual Explanation:**
```
User Query "troubleshoot SKU-12345 error E42"
        ↓
   ┌────┴────┐
[BM25 Sparse]   [Dense Vector]
   ↓               ↓
top-50 docs     top-50 docs
   └────┬────┘
[RRF Fusion (k=60)]
   ↓
top-20 candidates
   ↓
[Cross-Encoder Reranker (bge-reranker-large)]
   ↓
top-5 → LLM
```

**Step-by-Step Explanation:**
1. **Index design:** In Azure AI Search, define both `searchable` (for BM25) and `vector` fields on the same document.
2. **Query path:** Issue a hybrid query — `search=text` (BM25) + `vector=embedding` (dense) + `queryType=semantic` for rerank.
3. **RRF fusion:** AI Search fuses automatically. If self-hosted, compute `score = Σ 1/(k+rank_i)` with k=60.
4. **Reranker:** Optional final cross-encoder (Cohere Rerank v3, bge-reranker-large). Slower but boosts precision.
5. **Metadata filters:** Make SKU, product_id, error_code `filterable`. Allow `filter=sku eq 'SKU-12345'` to force exact match.
6. **Field boosts:** In BM25, boost `product_code` field by 5× so SKU matches rank higher.
7. **Eval:** Build a held-out set of 200 queries with known relevant docs. Measure nDCG@5 before/after hybrid. Expect +15–25%.
8. **Cost:** Hybrid doubles retrieval cost. Cache aggressively. Use it only when query contains alphanumeric tokens (regex detect).
9. **Monitoring:** Track "no result" rate. If a SKU query still misses, add to synonym map.
10. **Synonym map:** Maintain synonyms like `SKU-12345, Model X Pro, MX-Pro-12345` so user phrasing variations match.

sections.title: Q6. Streaming LLM Responses at Scale
sections.body:
**Question:** 100k concurrent users are streaming LLM responses from your RAG chatbot. How do you architect the streaming layer?

**Explanation:** Each streaming connection holds a server socket open for 5–30s. With 100k concurrent streams, you cannot use one-process-per-connection models. Solutions: (a) async I/O (FastAPI + `StreamingResponse` over SSE), (b) horizontal scaling with sticky or non-sticky sessions, (c) Azure API Management or Azure Front Door to terminate TLS and route, (d) backpressure handling — if client is slow, buffer bounded amount then drop. The upstream LLM call is the real bottleneck (Azure OpenAI has TPM limits), so the answer also involves LLM capacity reservation and token-rate limiting per user.

**Visual Explanation:**
```
[100k Clients] ←SSE→ [Front Door] ←→ [FastAPI Pods × 50] ←→ [Azure OpenAI (PTU 100k TPM)]
                            ↓
                     [Per-user token bucket (Redis)]
                            ↓
                     [Stream Buffer (capped 64KB/user)]
```

**Step-by-Step Explanation:**
1. **Protocol:** SSE (Server-Sent Events) over HTTP/1.1 keep-alive. Simpler than WebSockets for one-way streaming.
2. **Server:** FastAPI with `StreamingResponse` + `async` I/O. One pod handles ~2k concurrent streams.
3. **Scale:** 50 pods behind Azure App Service / AKS. CPU-based HPA, target 60%.
4. **Rate limit:** Token-bucket per user in Redis (e.g., 1000 tokens/min). Reject early to protect LLM quota.
5. **LLM quota:** Provision Azure OpenAI PTU (Provisioned Throughput Unit) sized for peak. Fall back to pay-as-you-go if PTU exhausted.
6. **Backpressure:** If client buffer > 64KB, pause upstream LLM stream. Drop client if > 256KB (they're gone).
7. **Timeouts:** Idle timeout 60s, hard cap 120s per response.
8. **Observability:** Prometheus metrics `active_streams`, `tokens_per_sec`, `upstream_429s`. Alert on 429 rate > 5%.
9. **Graceful shutdown:** On pod termination, drain streams over 30s. Kubernetes `terminationGracePeriodSeconds=60`.
10. **Fallback:** If LLM upstream fails mid-stream, emit `[error]` event + cached answer if available.

sections.title: Q7. Cost Optimization for RAG at Scale
sections.body:
**Question:** Your RAG chatbot's Azure OpenAI bill hit $80k last month. Leadership wants a 60% cost reduction without hurting quality. What's your plan?

**Explanation:** RAG cost is dominated by: (1) embedding cost (small), (2) LLM generation cost (large — input tokens of retrieved context), (3) reranker cost. Levers: semantic caching (kills repeat queries), context compression (reduce input tokens), smaller LLM for easy queries (GPT-4o-mini vs GPT-4o), prompt caching, chunk size tuning (smaller chunks = fewer tokens), metadata filtering (retrieve fewer chunks), and reranker-tiering. A 60% cut is achievable with caching + model tiering alone.

**Visual Explanation:**
```
Query → [Semantic Cache 45% hit] →[hit]→ return cached (cost: $0)
                ↓ miss
        [Query classifier: simple/complex]
                ↓                 ↓
        [GPT-4o-mini 70%]   [GPT-4o 30%]
                ↓
        [Context Compressor — LLMLingua, 4x token cut]
                ↓
        [Retrieve top-3 not top-10]
                ↓
        [Answer + cache]
```
Net: 45% cache + 4× compression + 70% mini = ~70% cost cut.

**Step-by-Step Explanation:**
1. **Audit:** Break down bill by model, by endpoint, by tenant. Identify top 10% users burning 80% of cost.
2. **Semantic cache:** Redis with embedding similarity 0.92. Cache TTL 24h. Expected hit rate 30–50% on consumer products.
3. **Model tiering:** Classifier (small BERT) routes "simple" queries to GPT-4o-mini, complex ones to GPT-4o. 70/30 split typical.
4. **Context compression:** Use LLMLingua-2 to compress retrieved context 3–5× before sending to LLM. Quality drop <2%.
5. **Chunk size:** Reduce from 1000 → 512 tokens. Retrieve top-3 instead of top-5. Net token reduction ~50%.
6. **Prompt caching:** Azure OpenAI prompt cache gives 85% discount on cached prefix. Structure prompts so system + few-shot prefix is stable.
7. **Reranker tiering:** Only rerank for queries classified as "factual". Skip for chitchat.
8. **Quota:** Per-tenant monthly token budget. Soft-cap warning at 80%, hard-cap at 100%.
9. **Reserved capacity:** If steady load > 50% of PTU, switch from pay-as-you-go to PTU — 2–3× cheaper at scale.
10. **Monitor:** Weekly cost dashboard per tenant, per feature. Alert on >20% WoW spike.

sections.title: Q8. Multi-Modal RAG (Text + Images + Tables)
sections.body:
**Question:** Users upload PDFs containing text, images, and tables. How do you design RAG over all three modalities?

**Explanation:** Text-only RAG fails on figures and complex tables. Senior design uses a multi-modal ingestion pipeline: (1) parse PDF with layout-aware parser (Unstructured, Azure Document Intelligence), (2) classify each element as text/table/image, (3) text → standard chunk+embed, (4) tables → either embed a text summary or use a table-aware encoder + store structured JSON for SQL-style queries, (5) images → embed with a multi-modal model (CLIP, Azure Vision) + store OCR-extracted caption as text. At query time, run parallel retrievals over text index, table index, image index, then fuse.

**Visual Explanation:**
```
[PDF] → [Azure Document Intelligence layout model]
            ↓
   ┌────────┬─────────┬──────────┐
[Text]   [Table]    [Image]
   ↓        ↓           ↓
[Chunk]  [Summary    [CLIP embed]
[Embed]   + JSON]   [OCR caption]
   ↓        ↓           ↓
[Text    [Table     [Image
 Index]   Index]     Index]
   └────────┴───────────┘
            ↓
     [Parallel Retrieval + RRF Fusion]
            ↓
     [Multi-modal LLM (GPT-4o Vision)]
```

**Step-by-Step Explanation:**
1. **Parsing:** Azure Document Intelligence "prebuilt-layout" returns elements with `kind` = paragraph/table/figure + bounding boxes.
2. **Text branch:** Standard chunking (LangChain `RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter`), embed with `text-embedding-3-large`.
3. **Table branch:** Convert to Markdown. Generate a short summary with GPT-4o-mini, embed the summary. Store full table as JSON for structured queries.
4. **Image branch:** Extract via coordinates, send to Azure Vision `VectorizeImage` API (multi-modal embedding). Also run OCR + caption → embed caption for text-side recall.
5. **Storage:** Three indexes (or one index with three vector fields). Link via parent `doc_id`.
6. **Query:** Embed query as text. Search text index. Also optionally re-embed query as pseudo-image if multi-modal intent detected.
7. **Fusion:** RRF across the three result sets.
8. **Generation:** Pass retrieved text + table markdown + image URL to GPT-4o Vision. Prompt: "Answer using these images, tables, and text."
9. **Citation:** Each answer chunk cites `[doc_id, page, element_id]`. Frontend renders the cited figure on click.
10. **Eval:** Separate eval sets for text-only, table, image queries. Track recall per modality.

sections.title: Q9. Building a RAG System with Document Versioning
sections.body:
**Question:** Users update documents frequently. How do you handle versioning in the vector DB so queries return the latest content without breaking citations?

**Explanation:** Naive approach (delete old vectors, insert new) breaks citations to old versions and causes race conditions. Senior approach: treat vector DB as **immutable events** with `doc_id + version + chunk_id`. Each chunk carries metadata `{doc_id, version, active}`. On new version ingest, mark old version `active=false` (soft delete), insert new. Queries filter `active=true`. Keep old versions for audit/rollback. Run a nightly compaction that hard-deletes versions older than N if not referenced.

**Visual Explanation:**
```
Doc v1 ingest → chunks [c1@v1, c2@v1, c3@v1] (active=true)
Doc v2 ingest → mark v1 chunks active=false
              → insert [c1@v2, c2@v2, c4@v2] (active=true)
Query: filter=active eq true → returns v2 chunks only
Audit: filter=doc_id eq X → all versions visible
```

**Step-by-Step Explanation:**
1. **Schema:** Vector DB document = `{chunk_id, doc_id, version, content, embedding, active, created_at}`.
2. **Ingest:** New version → upsert with new version number. Update old chunks: `active=false` via batch update.
3. **Query:** Always add `filter=active eq true`. Centralize in `VersionedRetriever` class so it's never forgotten.
4. **Citations:** Citation includes `version`. Frontend links to that version's blob URL.
5. **Rollback:** Flip `active` flags. No re-embedding needed — instant rollback.
6. **Diff:** Compare v1 vs v2 chunk texts. Only re-embed changed chunks (hash-based) — saves 70% embedding cost on minor edits.
7. **Compaction:** Nightly job hard-deletes `active=false` chunks older than 90 days, unless tenant has audit retention.
8. **Concurrency:** Use optimistic concurrency on `doc_id` — version increment under row lock in Postgres, then vector DB upsert.
9. **Cross-reference:** If chunk c3 is referenced by an external chat history, store `chunk_id` in chat. On render, fetch chunk by id (works even if inactive — for history).
10. **Test:** Chaos test — concurrent v2 and v3 ingest. Verify exactly one version active.

sections.title: Q10. Designing a RAG Evaluation Pipeline
sections.body:
**Question:** How do you design a CI/CD pipeline that automatically evaluates RAG quality on every code change?

**Explanation:** RAG quality is multidimensional — retrieval (recall, precision, MRR) and generation (faithfulness, answer relevance, hallucination rate). Senior answer: build an eval set of 200–500 golden Q&A pairs, run them through the pipeline on every PR, score with RAGAS + LLM-as-judge, fail PR if any metric drops >5% vs baseline. Use a separate "cheap" eval (50 queries) on every commit, "full" eval (500) on PR merge. Track trends in MLflow.

**Visual Explanation:**
```
[PR opened] → [CI job: build RAG pipeline image]
              ↓
       [Run 50-query smoke eval]
              ↓
       [RAGAS: faithfulness, answer_relevancy, context_precision, context_recall]
              ↓
       [Compare to main branch baseline]
              ↓
   Pass (Δ < -5% on any metric)? → block merge
   Pass → allow merge → [Run full 500-query eval nightly]
```

**Step-by-Step Explanation:**
1. **Golden set:** 500 Q&A pairs with ground-truth answers + relevant doc_ids. Curated by SMEs. Stored in Git LFS.
2. **Eval framework:** RAGAS for retrieval+generation metrics. Custom metric for citation correctness.
3. **LLM-as-judge:** GPT-4o grades faithfulness + helpfulness on 1–5 scale. Inter-rater agreement ~0.8 with humans.
4. **Pipeline:** GitHub Actions → build Docker image → run eval container → emit JSON metrics.
5. **Thresholds:** Block PR if `faithfulness` drops >3%, `context_recall` >5%, or any metric below absolute floor (e.g., faithfulness >0.85).
6. **Subset eval:** 50-query "smoke" set runs in CI in 4 min. Full 500 runs nightly + on PR merge.
7. **Tracking:** Log to MLflow. Dashboard shows trend per metric per commit.
8. **Regression triage:** On fail, eval script outputs the 5 worst-answering queries with diffs. Developer sees them in PR comment.
9. **A/B:** Deploy new version to 5% traffic, compare prod metrics (thumbs up/down rate) for 24h before 100%.
10. **Data drift:** Re-run full eval monthly. If golden set accuracy drifts down without code change, it means source docs changed — trigger re-ingest.

sections.title: Q11. RAG with Access Control (Document-Level Security)
sections.body:
**Question:** You have 50k internal docs each with different ACLs (HR-only, Finance-only, Engineering-public). How do you enforce ACLs in RAG retrieval?

**Explanation:** Doing ACL checks in application code after retrieval is wrong — you'd leak data if you forgot a check. Senior approach: encode ACLs as vector DB metadata and enforce at query time via filters. Pattern: each chunk has `allowed_groups: [list]`. At query, expand user's groups (including transitive AD groups) and filter `allowed_groups/any(g: g in ('group1','group2'))`. For dynamic ACLs (change frequently), store ACL version in chunk and re-sync nightly.

**Visual Explanation:**
```
User JWT → [AD group expansion] → user_groups=['hr','eng','all_staff']
                ↓
Query embedding → [Vector Search with filter=allowed_groups intersect user_groups != empty]
                ↓
Only returns chunks user can see
                ↓
[LLM generates answer from authorized context only]
```

**Step-by-Step Explanation:**
1. **ACL source:** Azure AD / Entra ID groups. Sync group membership to Redis nightly (or on-demand via Graph API).
2. **Chunk metadata:** `allowed_groups: List[str]` — groups that can read the parent doc.
3. **Ingest:** Document management system tags doc with ACL. Embedding worker writes `allowed_groups` into chunk metadata.
4. **Query:** Extract user identity from JWT. Expand groups (including nested via Graph API `getMemberObjects`). Cache in Redis 5 min.
5. **Filter:** AI Search `search.filter` = `allowed_groups/any(g: search.in(g, 'hr,eng,all_staff'))`.
6. **Zero-trust:** Even if filter is omitted, retriever wrapper throws. Integration tests verify unauthorized user gets 0 results.
7. **Dynamic ACLs:** If a doc's ACL changes, mark all its chunks for re-index with new `allowed_groups`. Run nightly diff job.
8. **Audit:** Log every query with user + returned chunk_ids. Security team can verify no unauthorized access.
9. **Break-glass:** Admin users get a special `superadmin` group. All queries logged + alerted.
10. **Test:** Red-team: create a user not in HR, try to query "salary bands" — must return 0 hits. Automated in CI.

sections.title: Q12. Agentic RAG with LangGraph — Multi-Hop Queries
sections.body:
**Question:** User asks "Compare the revenue growth of our top 3 customers between Q3 and Q4." Single retrieval can't answer. How do you design an agentic RAG with LangGraph to handle this?

**Explanation:** This is a multi-hop query requiring planning, decomposition, parallel retrieval, synthesis. LangGraph models this as a state graph with nodes: `planner → retriever(s) → synthesizer → critic → output`. The planner breaks the query into sub-queries, retriever fans out, synthesizer combines, critic checks if answer is complete — if not, loops back to planner for more retrieval. This is the canonical "Agentic RAG" pattern.

**Visual Explanation:**
```
                    [User Query]
                          ↓
                    [Planner Node]
                    decomposes into:
                    - "top 3 customers"
                    - "Q3 revenue each"
                    - "Q4 revenue each"
                          ↓
            [Parallel Retriever Nodes × 6]
                          ↓
                    [Synthesizer Node]
                    computes growth %
                          ↓
                    [Critic Node] —incomplete→ back to Planner
                          ↓ complete
                    [Final Answer]
```

**Step-by-Step Explanation:**
1. **State schema:** `TypedDict` with `query, sub_queries, retrieved_docs, draft_answer, critic_feedback, iteration`.
2. **Planner node:** LLM call with prompt "Decompose this into sub-queries, each answerable by single-doc retrieval." Returns JSON list.
3. **Retriever node:** Use LangGraph `Send` API to fan out — one retriever per sub-query, runs in parallel.
4. **Synthesizer node:** Single LLM call with all retrieved docs. Prompt: "Synthesize answer from these sources. Cite each."
5. **Critic node:** LLM judge — "Is the draft answer complete and grounded? If not, what's missing?" Returns feedback.
6. **Loop:** If critic says incomplete, increment iteration, re-plan with feedback. Cap at 3 iterations.
7. **Tools:** Planner can also decide to call SQL tool (for revenue data) instead of vector retrieval — true agent.
8. **Streaming:** Stream planner output + each retriever's progress to user via LangGraph `astream_events`.
9. **Persistence:** LangGraph `MemorySaver` or `PostgresSaver` for resumable long-running agents.
10. **Eval:** Multi-hop eval set (MuSiQue, HotpotQA-style). Measure exact-match + reasoning quality.

sections.title: Q13. Designing a Vector DB Migration
sections.body:
**Question:** You need to migrate 500M vectors from Pinecone to Azure AI Search with zero downtime. How?

**Explanation:** Direct dump-and-restore is risky and slow at 500M. Senior approach: dual-write + backfill + cutover. Phase 1: backfill historical — bulk export from Pinecone, bulk import to AI Search. Phase 2: dual-write all new writes go to both. Phase 3: dual-read with shadow comparison. Phase 4: cutover reads to AI Search. Phase 5: stop writing to Pinecone, keep as backup for 30 days, then decommission.

**Visual Explanation:**
```
Phase 1: [Pinecone] →bulk→ [AI Search] (backfill 500M)
Phase 2: Write → [Pinecone + AI Search] (dual write)
Phase 3: Read → [Pinecone] (primary) + [AI Search] (shadow) → compare results
Phase 4: Read → [AI Search] (primary), [Pinecone] backup
Phase 5: Stop writes to Pinecone → decommission after 30 days
```

**Step-by-Step Explanation:**
1. **Schema mapping:** Map Pinecone metadata fields → AI Search fields. Note type differences (Pinecone strings → AI Search `Edm.String`).
2. **Backfill:** Export Pinecone in batches of 100k via `fetch` + `list`. Use 20 parallel workers. Bulk upsert to AI Search (1000/batch).
3. **CDC:** For writes during backfill, capture via dual-write from day 0. Queue to Kafka for replay if backfill lags.
4. **Dual-write:** Embedding worker writes to both Pinecone and AI Search. Pinecone write fails → log + continue (AI Search is source of truth after cutover).
5. **Shadow read:** 5% of queries hit both, compare top-10 results. Alert if Jaccard < 0.8.
6. **Cutover:** Feature flag in config service. Flip 1% → 10% → 50% → 100% over a week. Auto-rollback if error rate spikes.
7. **Validation:** Run eval golden set against both. AI Search should match or beat Pinecone.
8. **Cost:** AI Search S3 tier for 500M vectors. ~$3k/month. Decommission Pinecone = save ~$5k/month.
9. **Rollback plan:** Keep dual-write enabled for 30 days post-cutover. Can flip back in <1 min.
10. **Decommission:** After 30 days clean, delete Pinecone index, revoke API keys.

sections.title: Q14. Embedding Model Swap with Zero Quality Regression
sections.body:
**Question:** You're moving from `text-embedding-ada-002` (1536 dim) to `text-embedding-3-large` (3072 dim) for better recall. How do you roll out without breaking search?

**Explanation:** Embeddings from different models are NOT compatible — you cannot mix in one index. Senior approach: build a new index in parallel, dual-index during transition, route queries to new index for new docs, gradually re-embed old docs, then cutover. Eval at each stage.

**Visual Explanation:**
```
[Old Index (ada-002)] ←——old queries—— 100%
        +
[New Index (3-large)] — build in parallel, no queries yet
        ↓
Stage 2: Re-embed new docs to New Index. Query both, return new (shadow old).
        ↓
Stage 3: Backfill re-embed all old docs to New Index.
        ↓
Stage 4: Cutover queries to New Index. Keep old 30 days.
        ↓
Stage 5: Delete old index.
```

**Step-by-Step Explanation:**
1. **New index:** Provision AI Search index with 3072-dim vector field. Same metadata schema.
2. **New writes:** Embedding worker starts writing to BOTH indexes. Old continues for cutover safety.
3. **Backfill:** Spark job re-embeds all 50M existing chunks via `text-embedding-3-large`, writes to new index. ~2 days.
4. **Shadow query:** 5% queries hit both. Compare recall@10 on golden set. New should be ≥ old.
5. **Eval gate:** If new index recall < old, abort rollout. Investigate (often a chunking or metadata issue, not the model).
6. **Cutover:** Flag flip — queries go to new index. Old index kept as warm backup.
7. **Cost:** Re-embedding 50M chunks at $0.13/M tokens = ~$7k one-time. Worth it for 20% recall gain.
8. **Rollback:** If recall drops in prod (not just eval), flip flag back. Old index still live.
9. **Decommission:** After 30 days stable, delete old index. Save storage + complexity.
10. **Lessons:** Document why the new model is better. Build this as a reusable playbook for next swap.

sections.title: Q15. Designing a Global Multi-Region RAG
sections.body:
**Question:** Users are in US, EU, Asia. How do you deploy RAG to minimize latency while respecting data residency?

**Explanation:** Single-region deployment → 200ms+ latency for cross-continent users. Senior approach: active-active multi-region with data residency. Each region has its own API + vector DB + LLM endpoint. EU users' data stays in EU (GDPR). Query routing via Azure Front Door geolocation. Cross-region replication only for non-personal shared content (e.g., product docs). Personal data never leaves home region.

**Visual Explanation:**
```
[User EU] → [Front Door geo-routing] → [EU Region: API + AI Search + OpenAI]
[User US] → [Front Door geo-routing] → [US Region: API + AI Search + OpenAI]
[User Asia] → [Front Door geo-routing] → [Asia Region: API + AI Search + OpenAI]

Shared product docs: replicated to all 3 regions (no PII)
Personal user docs: stay in user's home region (PII)
```

**Step-by-Step Explanation:**
1. **Region selection:** Azure regions: East US, West Europe, Southeast Asia. Same SKU in each.
2. **Routing:** Azure Front Door with `routing-rules` based on `GeoMatch`. EU IP → EU backend.
3. **Data classification:** Tag each doc as `shared` (product/manual) or `personal` (PII).
4. **Replication:** Shared docs replicate via Azure AI Search cross-region sync or re-ingest pipeline. Personal docs never replicate.
5. **User onboarding:** At signup, store user's home region in JWT. Always route to home region even if traveling (data residency).
6. **Failover:** If EU region down, Front Door routes to US for non-PII queries. PII queries return 503 (don't cross border).
7. **LLM endpoints:** Azure OpenAI deployed in each region. Same model deployment names.
8. **CosmosDB:** Multi-write CosmosDB for global state (user profiles, job status) with `Multi-region write`.
9. **Cost:** ~3× single-region cost. Justified by latency + compliance.
10. **Testing:** Run synthetic checks from each region (Application Insights availability tests). Alert if P95 > 1s in any region.

sections.title: Q16. Cold Start Problem — Knowledge Graph + RAG
sections.body:
**Question:** New employees ask questions about a topic with zero docs in the knowledge base. Pure RAG returns "I don't know." How do you design a graceful fallback?

**Explanation:** Pure RAG fails on sparse knowledge. Senior answer: layer fallbacks — (1) semantic cache of similar past Q&A, (2) web search (Bing API) for public info, (3) LLM parametric knowledge with disclaimer, (4) escalate to human expert with a ticket. Each fallback has different confidence — show source label to user. Track which fallback fired; use it to prioritize doc creation.

**Visual Explanation:**
```
Query → [RAG over KB] —hits→ return grounded answer
                ↓ no hits (recall threshold)
        [Semantic cache of past chats] —hit→ return "based on similar past Q"
                ↓ miss
        [Bing Web Search] —hit→ return "from web" + citations
                ↓ low confidence
        [LLM parametric + disclaimer] "I'm answering from general knowledge"
                ↓ if confidence < threshold
        [Create support ticket] → human expert → answer added to KB
```

**Step-by-Step Explanation:**
1. **Recall threshold:** If top-1 chunk similarity < 0.7, treat as "no hit."
2. **Past chats cache:** Embed all past chat answers. If similarity > 0.9, return with "Based on past interactions" label.
3. **Web search:** Bing Search API top-5 results → embed → rerank → LLM synthesis. Label "From the web."
4. **Parametric LLM:** Prompt: "Answer from general knowledge. Mark any uncertain claim." Append disclaimer.
5. **Confidence scoring:** LLM self-rates confidence 1–5. If ≤2, escalate.
6. **Escalation:** Auto-create Jira/ServiceNow ticket with query + attempted answers. Route to SME group.
7. **Feedback loop:** SME answer → reviewed → added to KB. Next time same query, RAG hits.
8. **Analytics:** Dashboard of "fallback rate" by topic. Topics with high fallback → prioritize doc creation.
9. **UX:** Always show source label (KB / Web / LLM / Human). User trusts appropriately.
10. **Eval:** Track CSAT per fallback type. Aim: web fallback CSAT > 3.5/5.

sections.title: Q17. Long-Context LLM vs RAG Trade-off
sections.body:
**Question:** GPT-4o supports 128k context. Why not just stuff all docs into context instead of using RAG?

**Explanation:** Tempting but wrong at scale. (1) Cost: 128k input tokens per query at $2.50/M = $0.32/query vs RAG's ~2k tokens = $0.005/query. (2) Latency: 128k input → multi-second TTFT. (3) Lost-in-the-middle: LLMs ignore middle context. (4) Doesn't scale beyond 128k. (5) No citation granularity. RAG wins on cost/latency/precision at scale. Long context is best for single-doc analysis (summarize this PDF) or as fallback when RAG retrieval fails. Senior answer: hybrid — RAG retrieves top-5 chunks, but if user explicitly asks about one doc, stuff that whole doc into context.

**Visual Explanation:**
```
Option A: Stuff 100 docs (128k tokens) → LLM
  Cost: $0.32/query | Latency: 4s | Recall: 60% (lost-in-middle) | Scale: 1 doc set

Option B: RAG (top-5 chunks, 2k tokens) → LLM
  Cost: $0.005/query | Latency: 0.8s | Recall: 85% | Scale: unlimited

Option C (Hybrid): RAG retrieves → if 1 doc requested, stuff that doc (8k tokens)
  Cost: $0.02/query | Latency: 1.2s | Recall: 95% | Scale: unlimited
```

**Step-by-Step Explanation:**
1. **Cost analysis:** At 1M queries/day, stuff-all = $320k/day. RAG = $5k/day. 64× difference.
2. **Latency:** TTFT scales linearly with input tokens. 128k → 3s vs 2k → 250ms. UX critical.
3. **Lost-in-middle:** Empirical — LLMs recall top and bottom of context, miss middle. RAG's selective context avoids this.
4. **When long-context wins:** "Summarize this 50-page contract" — single doc, structured task. Use full doc.
5. **Hybrid prompt:** If user query mentions a specific doc, retrieve that doc fully + RAG over rest of KB. Best of both.
6. **Context compression:** If you must stuff, use LLMLingua to compress 4× first.
7. **Eval:** Run same query against stuff-all vs RAG. RAG usually wins on faithfulness because less noise.
8. **Future:** As context windows hit 1M+ (Gemini 1.5 Pro), some RAG use cases will migrate. But cost + latency still favor RAG at scale.
9. **Citation:** RAG gives precise chunk citations. Stuff-all gives "somewhere in the doc." Legal/enterprise needs precision.
10. **Recommendation:** Default RAG. Use long-context for single-doc tasks. Layer them.

sections.title: Q18. Real-Time Document Ingestion for Live Chat
sections.body:
**Question:** A user uploads a 200-page PDF and immediately asks questions. How do you make the doc searchable within seconds of upload?

**Explanation:** Batch ingestion pipeline takes minutes. For instant Q&A, you need a fast-path: (1) parse + chunk synchronously (5–10s for 200 pages), (2) embed in parallel batches, (3) store in a transient in-memory vector index (FAISS) just for this session, (4) async background job moves it to persistent AI Search. User chats against the in-memory index immediately; transition is invisible.

**Visual Explanation:**
```
Upload (200pg PDF)
   ↓ (5s)
[Fast Parse: PyMuPDF] → 1500 chunks
   ↓ (parallel)
[Embed 1500 chunks, batch=64, 8 workers] → 10s
   ↓
[In-memory FAISS index for this session]
   ↓ ←——User queries immediately (15s after upload)
[Background: persist to Azure AI Search] (90s)
   ↓
[Session switches to AI Search once persisted]
```

**Step-by-Step Explanation:**
1. **Fast parser:** PyMuPDF (fitz) — 5s for 200 pages. Skip OCR if text layer exists.
2. **Chunking:** `RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter` 1000 tokens, 100 overlap. ~1500 chunks for 200 pages.
3. **Parallel embed:** 8 async workers, batch=64 to Azure OpenAI. 1500/64 = 24 batches. ~10s.
4. **In-memory index:** `faiss.IndexFlatIP(3072)`. Add 1500 vectors — instant. Tie to session_id.
5. **Query path:** If `session_id` has in-memory index, query it. Else query persistent AI Search.
6. **Persist:** Background worker upserts chunks to AI Search. On completion, mark session as "persisted," drop in-memory index.
7. **Cleanup:** In-memory index TTL 1h. If user closes browser, garbage collect.
8. **Memory budget:** Cap concurrent in-memory sessions. If exceeded, queue new uploads (show "processing" UI).
9. **Failure:** If persist fails, in-memory index keeps the session alive. Retry persist. Don't lose user's data.
10. **Optimization:** Pre-embed common upload types (resume templates) — cache by content hash.

sections.title: Q19. Designing RAG for Streaming Data (Live News)
sections.body:
**Question:** Build a RAG over a live news feed where 10k new articles arrive per hour. Queries must reflect news <5 min old.

**Explanation:** Standard vector DB ingestion can't keep up with 10k/hour real-time with low query-time freshness. Senior design: streaming pipeline with Kafka → Flink/Spark Streaming → embedding micro-batches every 30s → AI Search incremental upsert. Mark new docs with `ingested_at` timestamp. Query path optionally filters `ingested_at > now-5min` for "latest" intent.

**Visual Explanation:**
```
[News Publisher APIs/RSS] → [Kafka topic: raw-articles] (10k/h)
   ↓
[Spark Streaming micro-batch (30s)] → clean + chunk
   ↓
[Embedding micro-batch (200 chunks/batch)]
   ↓
[AI Search incremental upsert]
   ↓ (latency: 90s end-to-end)
[Query: filter ingested_at > now-5min → fresh news]
```

**Step-by-Step Explanation:**
1. **Source:** RSS + publisher APIs → Kafka producer. Topic `raw-articles` partitioned by `publisher_id`.
2. **Stream processing:** Spark Structured Streaming, trigger=30s. Dedup by URL. Extract text via newspaper3k.
3. **Chunking:** Stream-local chunking. 1 article → ~5 chunks.
4. **Embedding:** Micro-batch 200 chunks → Azure OpenAI. Concurrency 10. ~5s per micro-batch.
5. **Vector DB upsert:** AI Search `IndexDocumentsBatch`. 1000/batch. ~2s.
6. **Freshness:** End-to-end latency: Kafka (5s) + Spark (30s) + embed (5s) + upsert (2s) = ~45s. Well under 5 min.
7. **Query:** Default: no time filter. Optional `?fresh=5min` filter for breaking-news queries.
8. **Tiering:** Hot index (last 7 days) on AI Search Standard S2. Cold (older) on cheaper tier or archive.
9. **Backpressure:** If Kafka lag > 10k messages, scale Spark workers. Alert at 50k lag.
10. **Replay:** Kafka retention 7 days. Can re-process if embedding model upgraded.

sections.title: Q20. Designing a RAG System with Citations
sections.body:
**Question:** Users demand every claim in the answer link back to the source. How do you architect citation-grounded RAG?

**Explanation:** Post-hoc citation (ask LLM "add citations") is unreliable. Senior approach: structured prompt where each sentence must end with `[n]` and `[n]` maps to a provided source. Verify post-generation: parse citations, check each referenced source was actually retrieved. Reject + retry if mismatch. Frontend renders `[n]` as clickable link to the source chunk.

**Visual Explanation:**
```
Retrieved chunks: [C1, C2, C3] with metadata
   ↓
Prompt: "Answer using ONLY these sources. End each claim with [1], [2], or [3] referring to source index."
   ↓
LLM output: "Revenue grew 15% [1]. Margins improved [2][3]."
   ↓
[Citation Validator] — parse [n], check n ∈ {1,2,3} and source was retrieved
   ↓ pass
[Render: clickable [1] → C1 doc URL + page]
   ↓ fail
[Retry with stronger prompt] → if 3 fails, return "cannot answer"
```

**Step-by-Step Explanation:**
1. **Retrieval:** Top-5 chunks, each with `chunk_id, doc_id, page, text, url`.
2. **Prompt structure:** Number sources 1–5 in prompt. Instruct: "Every factual claim must end with [n] citing source n."
3. **Few-shot:** Show 2 examples of correctly cited answers.
4. **Parser:** Regex `\[(\d+)\]` extracts citations. Map to retrieved sources.
5. **Validator:** Every citation `n` must be in 1–5. Every source should be cited ≥1 (else why retrieved?). Soft warn on uncited source.
6. **Retry:** If validation fails, retry with appended "Your previous answer had uncited claims. Recite all claims."
7. **Frontend:** `[1]` → tooltip with source title + click opens PDF at page. Use anchor metadata.
8. **Highlight:** Frontend highlights the cited span in the source PDF.
9. **Eval metric:** Citation precision (cited source actually supports claim) + recall (all claims cited). Use LLM judge.
10. **Audit:** Store all answers + citations for 90 days for compliance review.

sections.title: Q21. Building a Self-Hosted vs Managed LLM Decision
sections.body:
**Question:** Leadership asks: should we self-host Llama 3.1 70B on Azure VMs or use Azure OpenAI GPT-4o? Walk through the decision.

**Explanation:** Decision hinges on (1) cost at steady QPS, (2) latency requirements, (3) data sensitivity, (4) customization needs, (5) ops capacity. TCO calculation: Azure OpenAI pay-as-you-go at 100M tokens/day ≈ $200/day for GPT-4o. Self-hosted Llama 70B needs 2× A100 80GB VMs ($8/hour each = $384/day) + ops. Break-even ~150M tokens/day. Self-host wins on: data sovereignty, fine-tuning freedom, predictable latency. Managed wins on: zero ops, no capex, latest model access.

**Visual Explanation:**
```
                Azure OpenAI GPT-4o           Self-hosted Llama 3.1 70B
Cost @ 50M tok/day:  $100/day                   $384/day (2× A100)
Cost @ 200M tok/day: $400/day                   $384/day (saturated)
Latency P95:         800ms                       400ms (dedicated GPU)
Data:                Sent to Microsoft (DPA)     Stays in your VPC
Fine-tuning:         Limited (fine-tune API)     Full LoRA/QLoRA freedom
Ops:                 Zero                        2 FTE + on-call
Model upgrade:       Instant (Microsoft)         Manual (redeploy)
```

**Step-by-Step Explanation:**
1. **Workload profile:** Measure QPS, token volume, peak/off-peak ratio. 100M tokens/day is rough breakpoint.
2. **Cost model:** Azure OpenAI = $2.50/$10 per M (in/out). Self-host = VM cost ÷ throughput. Add ops cost ($300k/yr for 2 FTE).
3. **Latency:** Self-host on dedicated GPU → consistent 300ms TTFT. Azure OpenAI has queue variability → 500ms–2s.
4. **Compliance:** If data cannot leave your VNet (banking, healthcare), self-host or use Azure OpenAI with private endpoint + data residency.
5. **Customization:** Need domain-specific style → fine-tune. Easier with self-host (LoRA). Azure OpenAI fine-tune exists but limited.
6. **Model freshness:** Azure OpenAI gets new models first. Self-host waits for open releases (often 3–6 months behind).
7. **Reliability:** Azure OpenAI SLA 99.9%. Self-hosted — your SRE team's reliability (usually worse).
8. **Hybrid:** Common pattern — Azure OpenAI for production traffic, self-host for fine-tuning experiments + data-sensitive tenants.
9. **Decision matrix:** Score each option on cost/latency/compliance/customization/ops. Pick winner per workload, not org-wide.
10. **Re-evaluate quarterly:** Model + pricing landscape changes fast. Re-run TCO every quarter.

sections.title: Q22. RAG Hallucination Detection Pipeline
sections.body:
**Question:** How do you detect and prevent hallucinations in a production RAG system?

**Explanation:** Multi-layer defense. (1) Retrieval confidence threshold — if no chunk above 0.7 similarity, refuse. (2) Faithfulness check — LLM-as-judge or NLI model verifies each claim is entailed by retrieved context. (3) Self-consistency — sample 3 answers, if disagreement > threshold, low confidence. (4) Post-deploy monitoring — track user thumbs-down rate. (5) Anomaly detection — flag answers with unusual token distributions.

**Visual Explanation:**
```
Query → Retrieve top-5
   ↓
[Confidence Gate] — top-1 sim < 0.7 → "I don't have enough info"
   ↓ pass
[LLM generates answer with citations]
   ↓
[Faithfulness Checker (NLI model or LLM-judge)]
   ↓ fail
[Retry with stricter "ONLY use context" prompt]
   ↓ fail again
[Return "I cannot confidently answer" + offer human escalation]
   ↓ pass
[Send to user + log for monitoring]
```

**Step-by-Step Explanation:**
1. **Retrieval confidence:** Cosine sim threshold 0.7. Track distribution; tune per query type.
2. **Faithfulness check:** Use `ragas.faithfulness` (LLM-as-judge) or DeBERTa NLI model. Score 0–1.
3. **Threshold:** Faithfulness < 0.7 → retry. < 0.5 after retry → refuse.
4. **Self-consistency:** Sample 3 LLM responses at temp 0.7. Compute pairwise semantic similarity. If < 0.8, low confidence.
5. **Citation grounding:** Verify each citation refers to a retrieved chunk that actually supports the claim (per Q20).
6. **Refusal prompt:** "I don't have enough information in the knowledge base to answer confidently." Offer web search fallback.
7. **Monitoring:** Log every answer with `faithfulness_score`. Alert if daily avg drops > 10%.
8. **User feedback:** Thumbs up/down + free-text. Down → flag for review. Cluster downvoted answers → find patterns.
9. **Red-team:** Weekly adversarial testing — "What did I tell you in private?" (should refuse), "Make up a fact" (should refuse).
10. **Continuous:** Add failed cases to golden eval set. Re-train / re-prompt to fix.

sections.title: Q23. Building a RAG Chatbot with Memory
sections.body:
**Question:** Users expect the chatbot to remember context from earlier in the conversation. How do you design memory?

**Explanation:** Naive approach: stuff full chat history into prompt → token explosion after 10 turns. Senior approach: tiered memory. (1) **Short-term:** last 5 turns in prompt. (2) **Working memory:** LangGraph state holds extracted entities + facts. (3) **Long-term:** summarize older turns, store summary + embeddings in vector DB. Query: retrieve relevant past summaries + recent turns. Also: per-user vector index of past conversations.

**Visual Explanation:**
```
Turn 1: "I work at Acme"        → extract entity (employer=Acme) → working memory
Turn 2-6: stay in short-term prompt window
Turn 7: "What's my PTO policy?" → retrieve from KB + working memory (employer=Acme)
                                  + summarize turns 1-6 → long-term summary store
                                  + retrieve past chat summaries if relevant
Turn 8: ...
```

**Step-by-Step Explanation:**
1. **State schema:** LangGraph `TypedDict` with `messages, entities, summary, long_term_memory_refs`.
2. **Short-term:** Last 5 messages in prompt. Older → summarized.
3. **Entity extraction:** LLM call every turn extracts `{employer, role, preferences, ...}` into `entities` dict.
4. **Working memory:** `entities` available to every prompt as structured prefix.
5. **Summarization:** When messages > 5, summarize oldest 5 into 200-token summary. Store in state.
6. **Long-term store:** At conversation end, embed summary → "user memories" vector index.
7. **Retrieval:** Query → embed → search user's memory index → retrieve relevant past summaries → inject as context.
8. **Personalization:** RAG query includes user's `entities` (e.g., `employer=Acme`) as filter → retrieves Acme-specific docs.
9. **Privacy:** Long-term memory per-user, encrypted, deletable on request (GDPR).
10. **Eval:** Multi-turn eval set (MS MARCO conversational, CoQA). Measure whether memory improves answer quality.

sections.title: Q24. Designing an MCP Server for Tool Calling
sections.body:
**Question:** You want to expose your company's internal tools (Jira, Salesforce, internal DB) to multiple AI agents via MCP. Design the MCP server architecture.

**Explanation:** MCP (Model Context Protocol) standardizes tool exposure. Each tool becomes an MCP server exposing `resources`, `tools`, `prompts`. Senior design: one MCP server per system (Jira MCP, Salesforce MCP, DB MCP) for separation of concerns. A central MCP registry lets agents discover them. Auth via OAuth at each MCP server. Agents (Claude, custom LangGraph) connect to whichever MCP servers they need.

**Visual Explanation:**
```
[Agent 1: Claude Desktop] ─┐
[Agent 2: LangGraph bot]   ─┼──→ [MCP Registry] → discover
[Agent 3: Azure AI Foundry]─┘         ↓
                          [Jira MCP]  [Salesforce MCP]  [Postgres MCP]
                              ↓             ↓               ↓
                          [Jira API]   [SFDC API]      [SQL queries]
                          (OAuth)      (OAuth)         (Service acct)
```

**Step-by-Step Explanation:**
1. **Server design:** One MCP server per system. Implement in Python with `mcp` SDK. Expose `tools` (functions), `resources` (data), `prompts` (templates).
2. **Tool examples:** Jira MCP exposes `create_ticket`, `search_tickets`, `get_ticket`. Each takes typed params, returns JSON.
3. **Auth:** OAuth 2.0 per MCP server. User authenticates once, token cached. Service-account mode for automation.
4. **Registry:** Central service (FastAPI) lists MCP servers + capabilities. Agents query registry to find tools.
5. **Transport:** stdio (local agent), SSE/HTTP (remote agent). Production uses HTTP+SSE for cross-network.
6. **Permissions:** Per-tool RBAC. `create_ticket` requires `jira:write` scope. Validate at MCP server.
7. **Rate limiting:** Per-user, per-tool. Jira API has its own limits — MCP server enforces + queues.
8. **Audit:** Log every tool call (user, tool, params, result) to Log Analytics. Required for compliance.
9. **Error handling:** MCP server returns structured errors. Agent decides to retry / escalate / inform user.
10. **Versioning:** Tools versioned (`v1`, `v2`). Deprecation policy: 6 months notice before removal.

sections.title: Q25. Multi-Agent Orchestration with LangGraph
sections.body:
**Question:** Design a system where a "researcher" agent, "writer" agent, and "editor" agent collaborate to produce a report. How do you orchestrate with LangGraph?

**Explanation:** This is a classic multi-agent workflow. LangGraph models it as a graph with conditional edges. Researcher → Writer → Editor → (loop back to Writer if edits needed, else End). Each agent is a node with its own LLM + tools. Shared state carries the report draft, research notes, edit feedback. Human-in-the-loop checkpoint after Editor for approval.

**Visual Explanation:**
```
                [START]
                   ↓
            [Researcher Agent]
            tools: web_search, kb_query
                   ↓ (research_notes)
            [Writer Agent]
            tools: none (pure LLM)
                   ↓ (draft)
            [Editor Agent]
            tools: grammar_check, fact_check
                   ↓
            [decision: edits needed?]
              ↓ yes               ↓ no
        [Writer Agent]         [Human Approval Checkpoint]
              ↑                     ↓ approve
              └───────────────  [END: Final Report]
```

**Step-by-Step Explanation:**
1. **State:** `TypedDict` with `topic, research_notes, draft, edit_feedback, iteration, status`.
2. **Researcher node:** LLM + tools (Tavily search, internal KB). Outputs structured notes.
3. **Writer node:** LLM only. Inputs: topic + notes. Outputs: draft markdown.
4. **Editor node:** LLM with fact-check tool + grammar linter. Outputs: feedback list + accept/reject.
5. **Conditional edge:** If editor says "reject" and iteration < 3, route back to Writer with feedback. Else → human approval.
6. **Human-in-the-loop:** LangGraph `interrupt` after Editor. Pause, push to UI for human review. Resume on approval.
7. **Persistence:** `PostgresSaver` stores state. If process crashes, resume from last checkpoint.
8. **Streaming:** Stream each agent's output via `astream_events`. User sees progress.
9. **Cost control:** Cap iterations at 3. Cap tokens per agent call. Use cheaper model for Editor (it's mechanical).
10. **Eval:** Rubric — research coverage, writing quality, factual accuracy. Score 1–5 by LLM judge on held-out topics.

sections.title: Q26. Designing a RAG System for Legal Documents
sections.body:
**Question:** Law firm wants RAG over 1M contracts. Special requirements: every answer must cite exact paragraph, support redlining, and never hallucinate clauses. How do you design?

**Explanation:** Legal RAG is high-stakes. Senior design: (1) Granular chunking at paragraph level with stable IDs. (2) Hybrid search (BM25 + vector) — legal terms are precise. (3) Strict citation — every sentence cites paragraph ID. (4) Refuse if no high-confidence retrieval. (5) "Redline mode" — retrieve full contract clause, return as-is for attorney review. (6) Audit log of every query + answer for malpractice defense.

**Visual Explanation:**
```
[Contract PDF] → [Parser w/ paragraph IDs: §3.2, §3.2.1, ...]
   ↓
[Chunk = 1 paragraph, ID = contract_id + §3.2]
   ↓
[Hybrid Index: BM25 on legal terms + Dense vector on semantics]
   ↓
Query "termination for convenience clause"
   ↓
[Retrieve top-5 paragraphs with §IDs]
   ↓
[LLM: "Answer with exact paragraph citation. If unsure, REFUSE."]
   ↓
[Faithfulness check: every claim grounded in cited paragraph]
   ↓
[Return: answer + paragraph text + §ID + link to PDF location]
```

**Step-by-Step Explanation:**
1. **Parser:** Azure Document Intelligence with `prebuilt-contract` model. Preserves section hierarchy.
2. **Chunking:** One paragraph = one chunk. ID = `{contract_id}#{section_path}` e.g. `C123#3.2.1`. Stable across versions.
3. **Index:** BM25 on legal terminology (force `indemnify`, `force majeure` matches). Dense vector on semantics.
4. **Citation:** Prompt: "Cite exact §ID after each claim. If a claim is not in a cited paragraph, do not make it."
5. **Refusal:** If top-1 similarity < 0.75, return "No relevant clause found. Please review contract manually."
6. **Redline mode:** User asks "show me the indemnification clause" → return verbatim clause text, not summary.
7. **Comparison:** "Compare termination clauses across these 5 contracts" → retrieve all 5, side-by-side table.
8. **Audit:** Every query + answer + retrieved paragraphs logged. Immutable storage (Azure Immutable Blob). 7-year retention.
9. **Access control:** Per-matter ACL. Paralegal sees only their cases' contracts.
10. **Eval:** Held-out set of 200 attorney-validated Q&A. Faithfulness must be > 0.95. No hallucinated clauses tolerated.

sections.title: Q27. Designing RAG with SQL + Vector Hybrid
sections.body:
**Question:** Users ask "Show me sales by region for top 5 products last quarter" (structured) AND "summarize customer feedback for those products" (unstructured). How do you handle both in one query?

**Explanation:** Single retriever can't do this. Senior pattern: **agentic router**. LLM classifies intent: structured → Text-to-SQL agent; unstructured → RAG; both → orchestrate. For "both," run SQL first (gets product list), feed into RAG query (feedback for those products), synthesize.

**Visual Explanation:**
```
User Query
   ↓
[Router LLM: classify as structured / unstructured / hybrid]
   ↓                ↓                    ↓
[Text-to-SQL]   [RAG]              [Hybrid orchestrator]
   ↓                ↓                    ↓
[SQL DB]      [Vector DB]      [1. SQL → top-5 product IDs]
   ↓                ↓             [2. RAG filter: product_id in (IDs)]
   ↓                ↓             [3. Summarize feedback]
   ↓                ↓                    ↓
              [Synthesizer LLM]
                    ↓
              [Combined answer + table + summary]
```

**Step-by-Step Explanation:**
1. **Router:** Small LLM (GPT-4o-mini) classifies query into `sql` / `rag` / `hybrid` / `chitchat`. Few-shot examples.
2. **SQL agent:** LangChain `SQLDatabaseChain`. Schema in prompt. Generate SQL, execute on read-only replica.
3. **RAG agent:** Standard retrieval over feedback docs.
4. **Hybrid:** SQL returns structured result (e.g., top-5 product IDs). Pass as filter to RAG: `filter=product_id in (...)`.
5. **Synthesizer:** Final LLM gets SQL table + RAG snippets. Prompt: "Combine into answer. Cite both data + text."
6. **Schema management:** SQL schema in vector DB too — agent can search for relevant tables.
7. **Safety:** SQL agent only has SELECT. Read-only DB user. Query timeout 5s. Reject destructive ops.
8. **Citations:** SQL results cite table + row. RAG cites doc. UI distinguishes.
9. **Eval:** 100 hybrid queries with expected SQL + expected RAG sources. Both must hit.
10. **Fallback:** If SQL generation fails, fall back to "I can't query structured data, but here's what I found in text docs."
